contents.name: 264A Definitions
contents.support: diameter empty=0; diameter power covers and supremum over scales.

contents.name: 264A Definitions
contents.support: Finite-delta definition with arbitrary covering subsets; s=0 adaptation explicitly follows 264D(b).

contents.name: 264B Lemma
contents.support: Outer-measure axioms including countable-subadditivity proof at fixed scale.

contents.name: 264C Definition
contents.support: Caratheodory restriction of the outer function; the scaffold first defines the outer function.

contents.name: 264D Remarks (a)
contents.support: Arbitrary cover sets cannot simply be replaced by equal-diameter balls.

contents.name: 264D Remarks (b)
contents.support: Counting measure at exponent zero, with a warning about interpreting cover formulas too literally.

contents.name: 264D Remarks (c): completeness
contents.support: Caratheodory measures are complete.

contents.name: 264D Remarks (c): atomlessness and non-semifiniteness
contents.reason: The singleton-null consequence is elementary and used in countable nullity; the stronger no-atoms and non-semifiniteness classification needs the later measure-structure theory, not any proof on this page.

contents.name: 264D Remarks (d)
contents.support: Decreasing scales increase approximants, and dyadic scales are cofinal.

contents.name: 264E Theorem
contents.support: Positive-separation additivity and Borel measurability; existing metric criterion supplies the general theorem.

contents.name: 264F Proposition (a,b)
contents.support: Close all sets in near-optimal covers and intersect countable unions; identifies the induced outer measure.

contents.name: 264F Proposition (c)
contents.support: Borel sandwich modulo null sets under sigma-finiteness.

contents.name: 264G Lipschitz functions — Proposition
contents.support: Diameter inequality after intersecting cover sets with the map domain; counting case separately.

contents.name: 264G Lipschitz functions — inverse-map application
contents.support: Two-sided application to a similarity and its inverse yields exact scaling.

contents.name: 264H Theorem (isodiametric inequality)
contents.reason: MT-21 expressly declines the sharp isodiametric theorem and its symmetrisation proof. Coordinate boxes suffice for positivity; no scaffold proof needs the sharp constant.

contents.name: 264I Theorem
contents.support: Source proves exact normalisation and matching measurable domains; scaffold proves its proportionality part by the design-mandated uniqueness route.

contents.name: 264I Theorem — exact constant
contents.support: Exact 2^n/volume(unit ball) is mentioned as sourced but unproved, never used in the local proof.

contents.name: 264J The Cantor set — Proposition
contents.support: Exact unnormalised critical measure one.

contents.name: 264J proof (a,b)
contents.support: 2^m stage intervals, each length 3^-m, give cost one.

contents.name: 264J proof (c,d)
contents.support: Concave-power gap inequality and full-cylinder counting; adapted to the already constructed Cantor measure.

contents.name: 264J proof (a,d): stage intervals
contents.support: Geometric construction intervals matched to the existing Cantor-function endpoint values; source counting is not itself a construction of the library measure.

contents.name: 264K General metric spaces
contents.support: Same construction on general metric spaces, including inf empty=infinity if no countable small cover exists.

contents.name: 264X Basic exercises (a)
contents.support: Fixed-scale outer measure and its zero sets; the content version is also in Bishop–Peres 1.2.6.

contents.name: 264X Basic exercises (b)
contents.support: Metric criterion already published; no duplicate criterion minted.

contents.name: 264X Basic exercises (c,d)
contents.support: Open/closed cover variants and G_delta equal-measure hulls.

contents.name: 264X Basic exercises (e)
contents.support: Finite measure at r forces zero at larger r.

contents.name: 264X Basic exercises (f)(i)
contents.support: General BV graph bound specialised to Lipschitz functions; the sharper sqrt(1+L^2) bound follows directly from 264G.

contents.name: 264X Basic exercises (f)(ii)
contents.reason: The Cantor-function graph measure exactly two is a separate non-Lipschitz graph calculation. The prescribed graph example is Lipschitz; no such equality is used in its proof.

contents.name: 264Y Further exercises (f)(i)
contents.support: Outer Hausdorff measure agrees between metric subspaces and their ambient space.

contents.name: 264Y Further exercises (f)(ii)
contents.reason: The full subspace-measure domain comparison has additional measurability or finite-measure assumptions; only the unrestricted outer-value comparison (i) is needed here.

contents.name: 264Y Further exercises (j)(i)
contents.support: General metric Lipschitz inequality combined with the critical exponent gives dimension monotonicity.

contents.name: 264Y Further exercises (j)(ii)
contents.reason: Measurability of Lipschitz images of arbitrary finite measurable sets requires completeness and compact approximation. The scaffold works with outer values for arbitrary images and does not require this additional result.

contents.name: 264Y Further exercises (k)
contents.support: Critical exponent in [0,infinity] for arbitrary metric spaces.

contents.name: Chapter 26 introduction; 265A Normalized Hausdorff measure (opening)
contents.support: Fremlin separates geometric construction from the next section on parametrisation, with normalisation introduced there. Orientation only; no area formula claimed.

contents.name: 1.2 Hausdorff measure: equations (1.12)–(1.14)
contents.support: Scale covers, outer measure and crossover exponent; strict positive diameter convention translated explicitly.

contents.name: 1.2 Hausdorff measure: cube estimate
contents.support: Subdivision gives finite H^n on the unit cube; elementary coordinate-volume lower bound is a local weaker form of the later volume comparison.

contents.name: 1.2 Hausdorff measure: s-sets
contents.support: Finite positive measure at the critical exponent is stronger than merely having that dimension.

contents.name: 1.2 Hausdorff measure: generalized gauge measures
contents.reason: General gauges refine dimension beyond power exponents; this page fixes diameter powers and none of its examples requires gauge measures.

contents.name: 1.2 Hausdorff measure: Besicovitch continuum partition observation
contents.reason: Partitioning arbitrary sets into continuum many equal-dimension pieces is a distinct descriptive-set-theoretic result; elementary explicit crossover witnesses serve the present scope.

contents.name: Theorem 1.6(a)
contents.support: Near-optimal open covers yield G_delta hulls.

contents.name: Theorem 1.6(b)
contents.support: Finite measurable sets contain F_sigma cores and closed approximants.

contents.name: Lemma 1.8
contents.support: Map cover sets and compare powers of diameters.

contents.name: 1.4 Lebesgue measure: opening through the H^1 comparison
contents.support: Intervals and their small subdivisions give equality of length outer measures.

contents.name: 1.5 Calculation of Hausdorff dimensions and measures: Theorem 1.14
contents.support: Exact middle-third Cantor critical measure and dimension; full proof read through its final square.

sources.title: Christopher J. Bishop and Yuval Peres, Fractals in Probability and Analysis
sources.locator: Contents pp.vii–ix (navigation); §1.2 pp.4–9 in full; §1.3 opening through Example 1.3.2 pp.9–12; Example 1.3.4 pp.15–16; Example 1.4.2 p.19; Exercise 1.6 p.36

contents.name: 1.2 Hausdorff dimension and the Mass Distribution Principle
contents.support: Countable arbitrary covers; content and small-scale Hausdorff measure.

contents.name: Definition 1.2.1
contents.support: Content-null definition translated to equivalent measure-null definition via Proposition 1.2.6.

contents.name: Definition 1.2.2
contents.support: Caratheodory measurable sets already defined.

contents.name: Definition 1.2.3
contents.support: Metric outer measure already defined.

contents.name: Theorem 1.2.4
contents.support: Metric outer measures measure Borel sets; instantiated for H^s using the existing theorem.

contents.name: 1.2 gauge function paragraph
contents.reason: The text flags gauges for later applications; power gauges are the fixed scope here and no gauge-exact example is required.

contents.name: Lemma 1.2.5
contents.support: Uniform scale factor epsilon^(beta-alpha) makes larger exponents null.

contents.name: Proposition 1.2.6: null-set equivalence
contents.support: Small total power-cost forces small diameters for positive exponent; zero exponent handled separately.

contents.name: Proposition 1.2.6: critical exponent
contents.support: Equivalent infimum and supremum formulas, retaining explicit empty-ray conventions.

contents.name: Equation (1.2.3): comparison to Minkowski dimensions
contents.reason: Minkowski dimension introduces a second dimension theory. The current page only needs arbitrary-diameter covers and Hausdorff dimension, and derives all upper bounds directly.

contents.name: Example 1.2.7: countable sets
contents.support: Countable sets have Hausdorff dimension zero.

contents.name: Example 1.2.7: countable sets applied to a dense set
contents.support: Specialise the countable argument to Q; density comes from the library.

contents.name: Example 1.2.7: Minkowski comparison for {0,1,1/2,...}
contents.reason: The compact sequence has Minkowski dimension 1/2, but this comparison needs the omitted Minkowski definition. Its Hausdorff-null conclusion is included.

contents.name: Lemma 1.2.8 (Mass Distribution Principle)
contents.support: Borel mass bounds summed across covers give a lower Hausdorff bound; local version uses sufficiently small covers and outer mass for arbitrary U.

contents.name: 1.2 positive Lebesgue measure consequence after Lemma 1.2.8
contents.support: Positive ambient volume implies full ambient dimension.

contents.name: 1.2 positive Lebesgue measure consequence after Lemma 1.2.8
contents.support: Apply full-dimension consequence to the existing fat Cantor set; local stage-length computation gives its positive measure.

contents.name: Example 1.2.9: four-corner planar Cantor set
contents.reason: The prescribed explicit planar computation is the Sierpinski gasket of Example 1.3.4. This second planar construction is not needed for any proof; its mass-distribution strategy is used for the chosen gasket.

contents.name: Example 1.2.10: von Koch snowflake
contents.reason: A snowflake curve construction and dimension computation would add a second self-similar planar example beyond the required gasket. It is not used for the metric/topology counterexample, which has an elementary metric witness.

contents.name: 1.2 Weierstrass-function paragraph
contents.support: Historical graph-dimension discussion is orientation, not a local theorem or an up-to-date claim of open status.

contents.name: 1.2 Brownian graph paragraph
contents.reason: Almost-sure Brownian graph dimension requires the stochastic-process development and is not a prerequisite of the deterministic examples.

contents.name: 1.3 Sets defined by digit restrictions: b-adic grid comparison
contents.support: Intervals meet a bounded number of comparable dyadic cells, enabling direct mass bounds without Billingsley.

contents.name: 1.3 grid measure and grid gauge definitions (1.3.1)–(1.3.3)
contents.reason: The proof uses the elementary cell-count comparison inline; it does not need a second family of grid outer measures or general gauge measures.

contents.name: Definition 1.3.1
contents.support: The lower density is written directly as liminf of permitted-position counts; upper density/Minkowski use is outside this theorem.

contents.name: Example 1.3.2
contents.support: Binary digit series and nested interval construction; membership allows either endpoint expansion.

contents.name: Example 1.3.2: upper and lower Minkowski dimensions
contents.reason: Both density/Minkowski equalities belong to the second dimension theory. The source range also states the Hausdorff formula, which is proved in the selected Example 1.4.2 and included here.

contents.name: Example 1.3.4: Sierpinski gasket
contents.support: Three permitted binary digit pairs give log(3)/log(2); mass distribution proof is executed explicitly with a Lebesgue coding measure.

contents.name: Example 1.3.4: Cantor product and Sierpinski carpet
contents.reason: These are alternative permitted-digit matrices. The task calls for one explicit Sierpinski-type computation, supplied by the gasket; neither alternative is needed as a lemma.

contents.name: Example 1.4.2
contents.support: Hausdorff dimension equals lower permitted-position density; the source uses Billingsley, replaced here by uniform cell bounds and the already scaffolded mass principle.

contents.name: Example 1.4.2: nonsquare-position specialisation
contents.support: Density one and infinitely many forbidden positions; the zero-length covering estimate is explicit in the notes.

contents.name: Example 1.4.2: square-position specialisation
contents.support: Density zero but infinitely many freely choosable bits; direct injectivity accounts for endpoint ambiguities.

contents.name: Exercise 1.6
contents.support: Dimension of a countable union is the supremum of its dimensions.

contents.support: Countable union formula follows from countable subadditivity.

contents.name: 2.5 Snowflake transforms — Lemma 2.41

contents.name: 2.5 Snowflake transforms — topology and diameter paragraphs

item_support.support: For a metric space, extend the existing diameter to all subsets: empty has diameter 0, an unbounded subset has diameter infinity, and nonempty bounded subsets retain their established diameter.
item_support.proof_plan: See the item-specific checkpoint in frontier-33-batch-1.notes.md; no proof body is claimed completed.

item_support.support: For s>=0 and 0<delta<=infinity, H^s_delta(A) is the infimum of sums of diameter(U)^s over at most countable covers by nonempty arbitrary sets of diameter <=delta. Empty cover allowed; 0^0=1 for nonempty singleton cover sets; infinity^0=1. Define H^s_infinity as Hausdorff content.
item_support.proof_plan: See the item-specific checkpoint in frontier-33-batch-1.notes.md; no proof body is claimed completed.

item_support.support: H^s_delta is monotone in A and nondecreasing as delta decreases; sup_delta>0 H^s_delta(A)=lim_k H^s_(2^-k)(A) in [0,infinity], including nonseparable spaces where some covers do not exist.
item_support.proof_plan: See the item-specific checkpoint in frontier-33-batch-1.notes.md; no proof body is claimed completed.

item_support.support: H^s(A)=sup_delta>0 H^s_delta(A), equivalently its small-scale limit, for finite real s>=0. Initially an outer set function on all subsets; its measurable restriction is a measure.
item_support.proof_plan: See the item-specific checkpoint in frontier-33-batch-1.notes.md; no proof body is claimed completed.

item_support.support: For any metric space and s>=0, H^s(empty)=0 and H^s is monotone and countably subadditive; each H^s_delta is also an outer measure.
item_support.proof_plan: See the item-specific checkpoint in frontier-33-batch-1.notes.md; no proof body is claimed completed.

item_support.support: H^s(A union B)=H^s(A)+H^s(B) for positively separated sets. Thus all Borel sets are Caratheodory measurable, and the restriction to the Caratheodory sigma-algebra is complete.
item_support.proof_plan: See the item-specific checkpoint in frontier-33-batch-1.notes.md; no proof body is claimed completed.

item_support.support: H^0(A)=#A if A is finite, and infinity otherwise; all sets are H^0-measurable.
item_support.proof_plan: See the item-specific checkpoint in frontier-33-batch-1.notes.md; no proof body is claimed completed.

item_support.support: Every subset A of a metric space has a Borel superset G with H^s(G)=H^s(A). H^s agrees with the outer measure induced by its Borel restriction. In Euclidean spaces one can choose G_delta hulls.
item_support.proof_plan: See the item-specific checkpoint in frontier-33-batch-1.notes.md; no proof body is claimed completed.

item_support.support: If E is H^s-measurable and sigma-finite, there are Borel E_minus subset E subset E_plus with H^s(E_plus minus E_minus)=0. For finite-measure Euclidean E there is an F_sigma core of equal measure and closed subsets with arbitrarily small measure deficit.
item_support.proof_plan: See the item-specific checkpoint in frontier-33-batch-1.notes.md; no proof body is claimed completed.

item_support.support: For s>=0, H^s_infinity(A)=0 iff H^s_delta(A)=0 for every finite delta>0 iff H^s(A)=0. This is not equality of the set functions.
item_support.proof_plan: See the item-specific checkpoint in frontier-33-batch-1.notes.md; no proof body is claimed completed.

item_support.support: For f:D subset X ->Y that is L-Lipschitz with L>0, H^s(f(A))<=L^s H^s(A), A subset D. At L=0 treat the singleton/empty image directly: H^s(image)=0 for s>0 and H^0(image)<=H^0(A).
item_support.proof_plan: See the item-specific checkpoint in frontier-33-batch-1.notes.md; no proof body is claimed completed.

item_support.support: If f scales all distances by c>0, H^s(f(A))=c^s H^s(A). Includes isometries, Euclidean translations and dilations. Computing measure in a metric subspace or its ambient space gives the same outer value.
item_support.proof_plan: See the item-specific checkpoint in frontier-33-batch-1.notes.md; no proof body is claimed completed.

item_support.support: If 0<=s<t and delta>0 finite, H^t_delta(A)<=delta^(t-s) H^s_delta(A). Consequently H^s(A)<infinity implies H^t(A)=0.
item_support.proof_plan: See the item-specific checkpoint in frontier-33-batch-1.notes.md; no proof body is claimed completed.

item_support.support: dim_H A=inf{s>=0:H^s(A)=0} in [0,infinity], with inf empty=infinity. In particular dim_H empty=0.
item_support.proof_plan: See the item-specific checkpoint in frontier-33-batch-1.notes.md; no proof body is claimed completed.

item_support.support: For d=dim_H A, H^s(A)=infinity for 0<=s<d and H^s(A)=0 for s>d. d also equals inf{s:H^s(A)<infinity} and sup{s:H^s(A)=infinity}, with sup empty=0. If 0<H^s(A)<infinity then d=s. At finite d the measure is not determined by d.
item_support.proof_plan: See the item-specific checkpoint in frontier-33-batch-1.notes.md; no proof body is claimed completed.

item_support.support: For arbitrary subsets A_k, dim_H(union_k A_k)=sup_k dim_H(A_k); inclusion implies monotonicity. Every countable set has dimension zero.
item_support.proof_plan: See the item-specific checkpoint in frontier-33-batch-1.notes.md; no proof body is claimed completed.

item_support.support: A Lipschitz map cannot increase Hausdorff dimension; a bi-Lipschitz bijection preserves it.
item_support.proof_plan: See the item-specific checkpoint in frontier-33-batch-1.notes.md; no proof body is claimed completed.

item_support.support: For n>=1, lambda_n^*(A)<=H^n(A) for all A subset R^n, and 1<=H^n((0,1]^n)<=n^(n/2).
item_support.proof_plan: See the item-specific checkpoint in frontier-33-batch-1.notes.md; no proof body is claimed completed.

item_support.support: For every A subset R, H^1(A)=lambda_1^*(A); the measurable domains and completed measures agree.
item_support.proof_plan: See the item-specific checkpoint in frontier-33-batch-1.notes.md; no proof body is claimed completed.

references.title: Fremlin 264I statement (weaker constant); design MT-21 prescribed uniqueness route

item_support.support: For n>=1 there is c_n in [1,n^(n/2)] with H^n(B)=c_n lambda_n(B) on Borel sets, and H^n(A)=c_n lambda_n^*(A) on all subsets. c_1=1. For n>=2 the exact c_n is not identified here.
item_support.proof_plan: See the item-specific checkpoint in frontier-33-batch-1.notes.md; no proof body is claimed completed.

references.title: Bishop–Peres §1.2 p.7 after Lemma 1.2.8; Falconer §1.2 p.8

item_support.support: dim_H R^n=n, and every subset of R^n has dimension <=n. Every set of positive Lebesgue outer measure has dimension n.
item_support.proof_plan: See the item-specific checkpoint in frontier-33-batch-1.notes.md; no proof body is claimed completed.

item_support.support: Let mu be a finite Borel measure, mu^*(A)>0, s>=0, C>0. If mu^*(U)<=C diam(U)^s for every nonempty U of sufficiently small diameter, then H^s(A)>=mu^*(A)/C and dim_H A>=s. For Borel A replace mu^*(A) by mu(A). A small-ball bound mu(B(x,r))<=C r^s suffices with the corresponding radius-to-diameter comparison.
item_support.proof_plan: See the item-specific checkpoint in frontier-33-batch-1.notes.md; no proof body is claimed completed.

item_support.support: Every level-m basic interval in the middle-thirds Cantor construction has Cantor measure 2^-m.
item_support.proof_plan: See the item-specific checkpoint in frontier-33-batch-1.notes.md; no proof body is claimed completed.

item_support.support: With s=log(2)/log(3), every interval I satisfies mu_c(I)<=diam(I)^s; hence every bounded nonempty U subset R satisfies mu_c^*(U)<=diam(U)^s.
item_support.proof_plan: See the item-specific checkpoint in frontier-33-batch-1.notes.md; no proof body is claimed completed.

item_support.support: For the middle-thirds Cantor set C and s=log(2)/log(3), H^s(C)=1 and dim_H C=s.
item_support.proof_plan: See the item-specific checkpoint in frontier-33-batch-1.notes.md; no proof body is claimed completed.

item_support.support: For S subset {1,2,...}, A_S={sum_(k in S) a_k 2^-k: a_k in {0,1}}. Digits outside S are zero; membership means some such expansion exists, so endpoint ambiguity is retained. Write a_S(n)=#(S intersect {1,...,n}).
item_support.proof_plan: See the item-specific checkpoint in frontier-33-batch-1.notes.md; no proof body is claimed completed.

item_support.support: A_S is compact and dim_H A_S=liminf_n a_S(n)/n. If the complement of S is infinite, lambda_1(A_S)=0. If S is infinite with infinite complement, A_S is uncountable.
item_support.proof_plan: See the item-specific checkpoint in frontier-33-batch-1.notes.md; no proof body is claimed completed.

item_support.support: At dimension 1 the possible critical measures include zero, finite positive, and infinity: use A_S with S the nonsquare positions, [0,1], and R, respectively.
item_support.proof_plan: See the item-specific checkpoint in frontier-33-batch-1.notes.md; no proof body is claimed completed.

item_support.support: Arbitrary covers are essential. Closed covers yield the same measure; ball-only spherical measure is comparable (H^s<=S^s<=2^s H^s for s>0) but need not equal it. H^s_infinity is content, not the small-scale measure. The Euclidean constant 2^n/lambda_n(B(0,1)) is a sourced identification not proved here and is not used.
item_support.proof_plan: See the item-specific checkpoint in frontier-33-batch-1.notes.md; no proof body is claimed completed.

item_support.support: Let D={(0,0),(1,0),(0,1)} and K={sum_(j>=1)2^-j d_j:d_j in D} subset R^2. Then dim_H K=log(3)/log(2), and its critical Hausdorff measure is finite positive (no exact value claimed).

item_support.support: With S the positive nonsquares, A_S is compact, dim_H A_S=1 and H^1(A_S)=lambda_1(A_S)=0. Thus dimension one does not imply positive length.

item_support.support: With S={k^2:k>=1}, A_S is uncountable and compact but dim_H A_S=0 and H^t(A_S)=0 for every t>0.

item_support.support: The restriction of the Cantor function to C continuously maps C onto [0,1], raising dimension from log(2)/log(3) to one.

item_support.support: False: H^s is countably additive on arbitrary disjoint subsets of R^n. Counterexample already at n=s=1.
